title: Linked list problems on LeetCode
overview: This module takes the singly linked list you built by hand and uses it to solve classic LeetCode problems: find the middle, detect a cycle, remove duplicates, reverse, check a palindrome and delete a node you only have a pointer to. Each file wraps the LeetCode `class Solution` with a `ListNode` definition and a small `main`, so you can run it locally. These patterns (counting, two pointers, re-linking `next`) come back in almost every linked list question.

concepts.explain: LeetCode gives you a ready-made node struct with `val`, `next` and three constructors. You only write the method inside `class Solution`; the judge builds the list and calls it.
Many problems become easy once you know the length. Walk the list once to count `size`, then walk again exactly the number of steps you need (for example `size/2` for the middle).
Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps each turn. If there is a loop, `fast` eventually laps `slow` and they meet; if there is no loop, `fast` falls off the end (hits `NULL`).
To remove the node after `temp`, point `temp->next` past it: `temp->next = temp->next->next`. Nothing else in the list has to move.
Recurse to the last node and make it the new `head`. On the way back, each node makes its next node point back to it (`tmp->next->next = tmp`) and cuts its own forward link (`tmp->next = NULL`).
Two lists intersect when they share the same node in memory. So compare pointers (`tempA == tempB`), not `val` — two different nodes can hold the same number.

concepts.term: Delete with only the node pointer
concepts.explain: If you can't reach the previous node, copy the next node's value into the current node and skip the next node. The list looks as if the current node was removed. It cannot work for the tail.

files.title: Middle of the linked list

problem.name: LeetCode 876 - Middle of the Linked List

files.what: Returns the middle node of a list; with two middles it returns the second one. It counts the nodes, then walks `size / 2` steps from the head.
steps: `get_size` walks from `head` to `NULL` and counts the nodes.
`middleNode` computes `idx = size / 2` (integer division).
A `for` loop moves `temp` forward `idx` times, starting at `head`.
`temp` now sits on the middle node, so it is returned.
`main` builds `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5` by hand and prints the middle node's value.
files.input_note: The list is built inside `main`; nothing is read.
files.output_note: With 5 nodes, `idx = 5/2 = 2`, so we step twice from `1` and print `3`. With 6 nodes, `idx` would be 3 and you would get the 4th node (the second middle).
files.watch_out: Integer division decides which middle you get. `size/2` gives the second middle for even lengths, which is what LeetCode wants.

check.q: For the list `10 20 30 40`, which value does `middleNode` return?
check.a: `size = 4`, `idx = 2`, so it steps twice and returns `30`.

files.title: Linked list cycle (fast & slow pointers)
files.what: Tells whether a list loops back on itself, using Floyd's fast and slow pointers.
steps: `slow` and `fast` both start at `head`.
While `fast` and `fast->next` are not `NULL`, move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps.
If they ever point to the same node, set `flag = true` and stop: there is a loop.
If `fast` reaches the end, the loop ends and `flag` stays `false`.
`main` tests a normal list, then links `n5->next = n3` to make a cycle and tests again.
files.output_note: First line `No` for the straight list `1..5`. Second line `Yes` after the tail was pointed back to node `3`.
files.watch_out: Check `fast != NULL` **before** `fast->next != NULL`; the order matters because `&&` stops early and protects you from reading `NULL->next`.

check.q: Why can't we just walk until `NULL` to detect a cycle?
check.a: In a cyclic list you never reach `NULL`, so the loop would run forever. Two pointers at different speeds are guaranteed to meet inside the cycle instead.

files.title: Remove duplicates from a sorted list

problem.name: LeetCode 83 - Remove Duplicates from Sorted List

files.what: Because the list is sorted, equal values sit next to each other. The code skips any next node whose value equals the current one.
steps: `temp` starts at `head`.
While `temp` and `temp->next` exist, compare `temp->val` with `temp->next->val`.
If equal, unlink the duplicate: `temp->next = temp->next->next` (and stay on `temp` — there may be more copies).
If different, move on: `temp = temp->next`.
Return the same `head`; `main` prints the list before and after.
files.watch_out: Only move `temp` forward when the values differ. If you always advanced, `1 1 1` would keep one extra `1`. (The skipped nodes are also never `delete`d here — fine for LeetCode, a small leak in real code.)

check.q: Would this code work on the unsorted list `1 2 1`?
check.a: No. It only compares neighbours, so the two `1`s (not adjacent) both stay.

files.title: Reverse a linked list (recursive)
files.what: Reverses the list in place with recursion: the last node becomes the head and every link is flipped on the way back.
steps: `reverseList` returns right away for an empty list.
`reverse(head, tmp)` takes `head` by reference so it can change the caller's head.
Base case: when `tmp->next == NULL`, `tmp` is the last node, so `head = tmp`.
Otherwise recurse on `tmp->next` first.
After the call returns, `tmp->next->next = tmp` makes the next node point back, and `tmp->next = NULL` cuts the old forward link.
`main` prints `1 2 3 4 5` then the reversed list.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) recursion stack
files.watch_out: Forgetting `tmp->next = NULL` leaves the old head pointing to the second node, which creates a 2-node cycle at the end of the reversed list.

check.a: So the base case can overwrite the caller's pointer with the last node; with a plain copy the new head would be lost.

files.title: Palindrome linked list (copy + reverse)
files.what: Makes a copy of the list, reverses the copy, and compares both lists value by value.
steps: `insert_at_tail` adds a new node after `tail` (and sets both `head` and `tail` for the first node).
`isPalindrome` walks the original and pushes each `val` into a new list `newHead`.
`reverse(newHead, newHead)` flips the copy with the recursive helper.
Two pointers `tmp` (original) and `tmp2` (reversed copy) move together; any different pair means `false`.
If the walk finishes without a mismatch, return `true`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the copy
files.output_note: `Is the list a palindrome? Yes` — the list reads the same backward.
files.watch_out: You must copy before reversing. Reversing the original list itself would destroy the order you want to compare against.

check.q: Why does the method copy the list instead of reversing the original?
check.a: Reversing in place changes the original, so there would be nothing left to compare the reversed order with.

files.title: Delete a node given only that node

problem.name: LeetCode 237 - Delete Node in a Linked List

files.what: You get a pointer to the node to delete but not the head. The trick: copy the next node's value into this node, then skip the next node.
steps: `node->val = node->next->val` — the node takes its neighbour's value.
`node->next = node->next->next` — the neighbour is unlinked.
The list now looks exactly as if `node` had been removed.
`main` builds `4 5 1 9`, deletes the node holding `5`, and prints before/after.
files.output_note: `Original list: 4 5 1 9` then `List after deletion: 4 1 9`. The node that held `5` now holds `1`.
files.watch_out: This trick cannot delete the tail (there is no next node to copy). The node that really disappears (old `n3`) is never freed in `main`.

check.q: Which physical node is actually removed from the chain when you 'delete' `5` in `4 5 1 9`?
check.a: The node that held `1` (the next one). The `5` node stays but its value becomes `1`.

files.title: Intersection of two linked lists (brute force)

problem.name: LeetCode 160 - Intersection of Two Linked Lists

files.what: Finds the first node that two lists share by checking every node of A against every node of B, comparing addresses.
steps: Outer loop: `tempA` visits each node of list A.
Inner loop: `tempB` restarts at `headB` and visits each node of B.
If `tempA == tempB` (same address), that node is where the lists join — return it.
If no pair matches, return `NULL`.
`main` builds A = `4 1 [8 4 5]` and B = `5 6 1 [8 4 5]` where the bracketed part is shared.
files.output_note: Both lists are printed, then `Intersection at node with value: 8` — the first shared node. Note the `1` in both lists is **not** the answer: they are different nodes with equal values.
files.watch_out: The cleanup comment is wrong: `delete common1` frees only that one node, not `common2`/`common3` (they leak). Faster idea to try: two pointers that switch to the other list's head at the end meet at the intersection in O(n+m).

check.q: Why is `tempA->val == tempB->val` the wrong test here?
check.a: Different nodes can hold the same value (both lists contain a `1`). Only the same address means the lists really share the node.

files.title: Swap the k-th node from start and end

problem.name: LeetCode 1721 - Swapping Nodes in a Linked List

files.what: Finds the k-th node from the front and the k-th from the back, then swaps their values.
steps: Count the nodes into `length`.
`frontNode` starts at `head` and moves `k-1` steps: the k-th node from the start.
`backNode` starts at `head` and moves `length-k` steps: the k-th node from the end.
`swap(frontNode->val, backNode->val)` exchanges only the values; links stay the same.
`main` uses `1 2 3 4 5` with `k = 2`.
files.input_note: The list and `k = 2` are fixed in `main`.
files.output_note: `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5` becomes `1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 5`: the 2nd from the front (`2`) and 2nd from the back (`4`) switched.

check.q: For a list of length 7 and `k = 3`, how many steps does `backNode` take from the head?
check.a: `length - k = 4` steps, landing on the 5th node, which is the 3rd from the end.

recap: On LeetCode you only write `class Solution`; `ListNode` and the list are given.
Count the length first when you need 'k-th from the end' or 'the middle'.
Fast/slow pointers detect a cycle in O(1) extra space.
Remove a node by re-pointing the previous `next`: `temp->next = temp->next->next`.
Recursive reverse: go to the end, then flip each link on the way back.
Shared nodes are found by comparing addresses, never values.

check_yourself.q: In the cycle check, what does it mean if `fast` becomes `NULL`?
check_yourself.a: The list has an end, so there is no cycle.

check_yourself.q: Which of this module's techniques cannot delete the last node of a list, and why?
check_yourself.a: The 'copy the next value and skip it' trick from Delete Node — the tail has no next node to copy from.

check_yourself.q: What extra memory does the palindrome solution use, and how could you avoid it?
check_yourself.a: A full copy of the list, O(n). You could instead find the middle, reverse only the second half in place, and compare the halves.
